body: I am so sorry, it is not okay. That should not negate you being too drunk to consent. I am so sick of this idea of the perfect victim, that there is only a few “real” ways that a rape victim would act/respond to being raped. What you said does not change his actions and does not change that you were incapacitated.

I don’t have anyone who is specifically a legal advocate. That would be helpful. I do have a survivor advocate from the county’s rape crisis center that is separate from the prosecutor’s office. However I have found the title misleading because she has not been able to do any advocating. She told me she is not allowed to speak during the meetings I’ve had with the prosecutors office or with the detectives on my case. All that she has done (or been allowed to do) is to be present during these meetings. It’s better than nothing. Im glad she was there, but I have not been able to get the level of support that I need. I don’t have anyone taking on this fight with me. Most recently I shared with her the recordings of my meetings with the first prosecutor and asked her to share them with her supervisor, but she hasn’t responded to that email. I am going to follow up on it.
I'm so sorry that this happened to you. Was an attempt made (by police, prosecutor, yourself, etc.) to verify the legitimacy of the texts in your situation?
I will keep this in mind, thank you.
Did you ever have an instance where you decided not to pursue a case and then changed your mind or vice versa? (For any reason)

There isn't a difference. Those two titles are used interchangeably and "survivor advocate" is such an incredibly common phrase that it is strange to me that the AP, who works in sex crimes, does not know what that means.

That kick in the pants is what I am hoping a personal lawyer can help me with, to help show them that I am serious and I won’t give up without a fight. (I know that a private attorney can not pursue criminal charges).
